title: Free Floating Nations: The Vehicle Loophole and the Ungoverned Lakes
body:
# Free Floating Nations: The Vehicle Loophole and the Ungoverned Lakes

## The Legal Foundation

The GLMZ Governance Consortium's territorial authority derives from the same principle that has governed land ownership since the concept existed: sovereignty attaches to ground. If you are standing on ground — or your structure rests on ground, whether that ground is dry land, lake bed, or ocean floor — you are within the territorial claim of whoever owns that ground. This principle is why Bathysphere Networks' subsurface installations are valid sovereign territory: they rest on the lake bed, which is ground, and Bathysphere holds a chartered claim to that ground. This principle is also why the GLMZ's authority extends to underwater structures. A city built on the floor of Lake Michigan is a city built on land that someone claims.

A city that does not touch the bottom is something else.

A structure that floats freely on the surface of a body of water — that is not anchored, not tethered, not resting on any territorial substrate — is, under the legal frameworks that the GLMZ Governance Consortium inherited from the collapsed American regulatory apparatus, a **vessel**. Vessels are governed by maritime law, not territorial law. Maritime law, in the GLMZ context, is administered by the Governance Consortium's Maritime Adjudication Board — a body that has eleven members, meets quarterly, and has a documented backlog of 4,200 unresolved cases stretching back to 2189.

The practical implication: a floating structure that is not touching the bottom is not subject to GLMZ corponation territorial authority. It is not subject to tier classification enforcement. It is not subject to sponsorship requirements. It is not part of the GLMZ.

## The Casino Precedent

This was not a new idea when the first Free Floating Nation declared itself in 2178.

The legal distinction between a vessel and a structure was already a century old by then — inherited from American state law, specifically from Indiana, which required casinos to be on water. The original interpretation was narrow: a barge floating three inches off the coast of Michigan City was technically a vessel and therefore exempt from Indiana land-use law, which was the point. The Michigan City casino fleet operated on this distinction for decades before the collapse of Indiana's regulatory apparatus made the distinction irrelevant for original purposes.

But the legal precedent survived. When the GLMZ's governance framework was assembled in the 2140s and 2150s, the maritime law inheritance was incorporated by reference — the Consortium's lawyers needed something to fill the regulatory gap on water, and maritime law was there. They incorporated it without fully considering what it implied.

What it implied was that anything which floated freely was a vessel. And a vessel could be very large.

The first deliberate exploitation of this — before the formal declaration of any Free Floating Nation — was a settlement called the **Drift**, assembled in 2151 from decommissioned Great Lakes cargo barges in the open water northeast of Milwaukee. The Drift's founders were former Sulfur Crown Agriculture indentures who had completed their contracts and found themselves without corponation housing, without Gray Zone community connections, and without the tier classification required to work in any Zone 8-10 corponation territory. They had no options on land. The lake had no territorial claimant in the relevant area.

The Drift was not elegant. It was a raft of barges connected by cable and rope, sheltering approximately 400 people, generating its own power from solar arrays, fishing the lake for food, and — critically — moving. The Governance Consortium's Maritime Adjudication Board sent a notice of jurisdiction inquiry. The Drift relocated 12 kilometers northwest before the inquiry could be formally served. The inquiry was filed as undeliverable.

The Drift is still operating. Population: approximately 14,000. They have moved 847 times.

## What Makes a Free Floating Nation

The legal definition that the GLMZ Governance Consortium has been unable to effectively challenge requires three conditions for a structure to qualify as a vessel rather than a territorial installation:

**1. It must be buoyant by design.** A structure that rests on the bottom and uses buoyancy to reduce weight on its foundation is not a vessel. A structure that floats freely with no contact with the lake bed qualifies.

**2. It must be capable of self-propulsion or free drift.** A structure that is permanently anchored to the lake bed is attached to the lake bed — and by extension to the territorial claim on that lake bed. A structure that drops anchor temporarily without establishing permanent installation does not lose vessel status under existing case law, though this remains actively contested. A structure that can move under its own power is unambiguous.

**3. It must not be physically connected to a structure with established territorial status.** A floating structure attached by bridge, tunnel, cable infrastructure, or utility connection to a corponation facility or land-based installation loses vessel status in proportion to the permanence of the connection. Temporary docking does not constitute connection. A power cable that runs to the lake bed and connects to Bathysphere Networks infrastructure is legally ambiguous and has been the subject of seven separate Governance Consortium rulings, each of which contradicts at least one of the others.

Structures meeting these three conditions are treated as vessels. A vessel that has declared a governance framework, established a permanent population, and registered with the Maritime Adjudication Board can petition for recognition as a **Free Floating Nation** — a vessel-state. The Board has accepted 23 such petitions. It has rejected 11. It has lost 4 in the filing backlog.

## The Spectrum of Free Floating Nations

Free Floating Nations range from barely-organized survival communities to functioning polities more sophisticated than some of the GLMZ's mid-tier corponation territories.

**Subsistence Floaters** are the smallest and most numerous: collections of barges, repurposed platforms, and improvised structures sheltering populations from a few dozen to a few hundred. They fish, trade with passing vessels, and move frequently to avoid both GLMZ enforcement and each other's territorial disputes. Most do not formally qualify as Free Floating Nations and make no effort to register with the Maritime Adjudication Board. The Board, for its part, makes no effort to find them.

**Established Floaters** have stable populations, defined governance structures, and sufficient resources to maintain their vessel systems indefinitely. The Drift is the archetypal established floater. Others include the **Pelagic Congregation** (religious community, Lake Michigan, population approximately 6,000, refuses formal registration on principle), the **Anchor Hold** (former Ringo Corponation contract workers, Lake Huron, population 3,200, operates a gray-market augmentation service that the Corponation has been attempting to shut down for seventeen years), and **New Łódź** (named for the Polish city, founded by second-generation Polish-Nigerian diaspora, Lake Michigan north of Milwaukee, population approximately 11,000, the most organized governance structure of any Free Floating Nation).

**City-Scale Floaters** are the entities that the GLMZ Governance Consortium finds most threatening and least able to address. The largest, the **Abyssal Platform Collective**, is not a single vessel but a coordinated fleet of 340 structures that travel together and constitute, by any reasonable measure, a small city. Total population: approximately 90,000. The Collective has its own currency, its own adjudication system, its own defense force (primarily automated), and its own diplomatic relationships — it has signed trade agreements with three GLMZ corponations and one Canadian territorial entity. The Governance Consortium does not recognize these agreements. The corponations do.

## The Anchor Problem

The most legally contested issue in Free Floating Nation jurisprudence is the anchor.

A vessel that drops anchor is not touching the bottom — the anchor is touching the bottom, and the chain attaches the vessel to the anchor, and the anchor is in contact with the lake bed, which is territorial substrate. The question of whether this constitutes "resting on" the territorial substrate has been argued before the Maritime Adjudication Board more times than any other single question in GLMZ maritime law.

The current state of the case law is incoherent. Six rulings hold that temporary anchoring does not affect vessel status. Two hold that any anchoring creates territorial nexus. One, issued by a Board member who has since been removed for reasons the Board has not disclosed, holds that the question depends on the intent of the anchoring party, which raises its own obvious evidentiary problems.

The practical result is that Free Floating Nations anchor whenever they want and move before any enforcement action can be formalized. The Maritime Adjudication Board's enforcement arm — a single vessel staffed by twelve people — has never successfully served a jurisdiction order on a Free Floating Nation that did not want to receive it.

## Bathysphere Networks and the Free Floating Nations

Bathysphere Networks' sovereign territory is the lake bed. Free Floating Nations live on the lake surface. These are different layers of the same body of water, and the legal relationship between them is not straightforward.

Bathysphere's subsurface data and power infrastructure runs beneath the entire GLMZ lake zone, including the areas where Free Floating Nations operate. Free Floating Nations that want connectivity — and most of them do — need to either access Bathysphere infrastructure or build their own. Building their own subsurface infrastructure would require claiming lake bed territory, which would expose them to GLMZ territorial authority. Most Free Floating Nations choose to access Bathysphere.

This gives Bathysphere a degree of leverage over Free Floating Nations that they do not advertise and do not forgo. Bathysphere sells connectivity to Free Floating Nations at rates that are nominally market-priced and functionally punitive compared to what they charge GLMZ corponation clients. The Free Floating Nations pay because the alternative is isolation. The GLMZ Governance Consortium is aware of this arrangement and privately considers it the most effective check on Free Floating Nation growth that currently exists.

Bathysphere, for its part, considers Free Floating Nation revenue streams among its most reliable — unlike corponation clients, Free Floating Nations have no leverage with which to renegotiate their contracts.

## Corponation Responses

The corponations have responded to Free Floating Nations with a combination of strategies that reflect their individual characters.

**Rictus Entertainment** operates the most aggressively positive relationship: they have established formal docking agreements with the three largest Free Floating Nations, which function as entertainment partnerships. Rictus content is distributed to FFN populations at favorable rates; in exchange, Rictus has access to populations that exist outside the GLMZ's tier classification system, which turns out to be extraordinarily valuable for content research. People who live outside the social order behave in ways that fascinate the people inside it. Rictus's most successful content franchise of the 2220s, *The Open Water*, is filmed almost entirely aboard Free Floating Nation vessels.

**Arcturus Defense Solutions** treats Free Floating Nations as ungoverned zone analogs — populations outside their security contract zone that are not their problem and not their responsibility. This is the official position. Unofficially, Arcturus has, on three documented occasions, provided security consultation services to Free Floating Nations threatened by other actors. The consultations were paid for in categories of goods that do not appear in Arcturus's official revenue reporting.

**Tessera Corponation** has petitioned the Maritime Adjudication Board seventeen times in forty years to tighten the definition of what constitutes a vessel. Twelve of these petitions were denied. Four are pending. One resulted in the ruling that anchoring does not affect vessel status, which was not the outcome Tessera intended and which they have been attempting to overturn ever since.

**Ringo Corponation** considers Free Floating Nations a leakage problem. Former Ringo employees who complete their indentures and cannot afford to remain in Ringo territory have a demonstrated tendency to join Free Floating Nation communities. Ringo has responded by tightening indenture exit terms in ways that the Maritime Adjudication Board has noted, in an advisory opinion, appear designed to prevent people from reaching the lake. The Board noted this. They did not act on it.

## The Michigan City Continuity

Michigan City's casino tradition did not end with the collapse of Indiana's regulatory apparatus. It evolved.

The three casino vessels that were operating under Indiana's maritime exemption in 2131 — when Indiana's state government formally ceased to function — found themselves in a legal vacuum. Their original exemptions had been granted by a state that no longer existed. Their territorial neighbors were either Gray Zone communities with no enforcement capacity or the nascent Ashgrave Materials industrial operation, which had no interest in casino regulation. The vessels continued operating.

By 2150, the Michigan City casino fleet had grown from three vessels to eleven. By 2175, it was formally recognized as the **Michigan City Compact** — the first entity to successfully petition the GLMZ Maritime Adjudication Board for Free Floating Nation status. The Compact's petition noted that its members had been operating as vessels for more than forty years under continuous maritime law precedent, that their economic activities generated value for the Zone 11 shore communities through docking fees and supply contracts, and that their formal recognition would reduce legal uncertainty for all parties.

The Board approved the petition in 2176. The Michigan City Compact is currently the oldest continuously operating Free Floating Nation in the GLMZ, with a population of approximately 22,000 distributed across 34 vessels. They still run casinos. They also run the most sophisticated gray-market financial services operation in the Corridor — the structural advantage of being legally neither corponation territory nor Gray Zone turns out to be enormously valuable when parties on both sides of a transaction prefer anonymity.
